extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator / general 18th-century literate public interested in manners, morals, and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted prescriptive principles and evaluative ideas found in early-18th-century Spectator essays and letters on conduct, leadership, parenting, marriage, and literary/dramatic criticism. Useful for understanding the author's standards for behaviour and taste in that periodical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental provision of lawful diversions for sons
rubrics_metrics.description: "The Skill therefore should, methinks, be to let a Son want no lawful Diversion, in proportion to his future Fortune, and the Figure he is to make in the World."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parents should supply sons with lawful amusements and suitable education proportional to their social position and expected fortune; withholding necessary diversions or education may push youths into excesses or criminal resourcefulness (e.g., becoming cheats or rascals). Example: narrowness in circumstances has made many youths, to supply themselves as debauchees, commence cheats and rascals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid parental neglect and self-interested exclusion of children
rubrics_metrics.description: "A Man may, if he will, let his Heart close to the having no regard to any thing but his dear self, even with exclusion of his very Children."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware parental behaviour that excludes or humiliates one's children for vanity or self-image (e.g., a father who affects being a fine gentleman and thrusts his son out of the gay world). Such conduct is morally blameable and harms children's prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as the primary quality in leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: "Justice is the first Quality in the Man who is in a Post of Direction;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person in authority should above all be just: keep accurate records (dates of commissions), dismiss those deficient in duty, promote according to order and merit, and so command the respect and submission of others. Justice makes decision-making short and effective and creates trust so that private petitions and reconciliations are respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion and preferment by merit, not favouritism
rubrics_metrics.description: His Affection was no Step to their Preferment, tho' it was to their Reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those in power should prefer and promote according to merit and established order (e.g., 'according to the Order of Battel'), not by personal affection or courtly favour; extraordinary merit should be recommended appropriately (to the sovereign) rather than rewarded by partiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove and reassign the idle or merely showy rather than reward them
rubrics_metrics.description: He had an excellent Manner of getting rid of such whom he observed were good at 'an Halt'... These Fellows were also recommended to the King, and taken off of the General's hands into Posts wherein Diligence and common Honesty were all that were necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prudent governor reassigns personnel according to true aptitude: those content with harmless mediocrity should be placed where diligence and honesty suffice, while positions requiring vigor and reputation should be held to higher standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers should not delight in buffoons, coxcombs, and ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When Leo X. ... carried it so far, that his whole Delight was in finding out new Fools, and... playing them off and making them shew themselves to advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sovereign's indulgence of fools and affectation undermines public reverence; favouring buffoons and coxcombs risks reducing the authority of office to mere spectacle and invites contempt for customary insignia and traditional dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not value mere solemn appearances over substance
rubrics_metrics.description: The first minister would let nothing come near him but what bore the most profound Face of Wisdom and Gravity... a Pair of Spectacles tied on their Noses... compleated the Dress of those who made their court...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A warning against mistaking superficial signs of gravity (dress, affectation) for real competence or wisdom; courtly postures and trappings can be gamed (an example: a blunt honest officer succeeded by adopting the farce) and should not substitute for substantive qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of time and place as a literary/dramatic principle
rubrics_metrics.description: P. S. 'I have heard our Criticks in the Coffee-houses hereabout talk mightily of the Unity of Time and Place: According to my Notion of the Matter, I have endeavoured at something like it in the Beginning of my Epistle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity of time and place is presented as a recognized critical expectation among contemporary critics; authors may deliberately attempt to observe it (e.g., structuring an epistle to approximate that unity) as an aesthetic choice responding to critical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dream/fiction in satire to exaggerate or expose social foibles
rubrics_metrics.description: "I fell into the following Dream... I cannot conclude my Letter... without telling thee one very odd Whim in this my Dream..." and the author's note: "...in order to abuse them, the Writer is obliged to have recourse to Dream and Fiction."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical critique can legitimately employ dream or fictional scenarios to magnify and expose social behaviours and vices; the author notes that to lampoon a class (here, the sex) one sometimes must resort to invented or dream-like situations rather than factual reportage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage and parenthood as sources of authority and moral education
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are two... Pleasures... nothing is more gratifying to the Mind of Man than Power or Dominion; and this... as I am the Father of a Family... I look upon my self as a most insufferable Coxcomb, did I endeavour to maintain that Cuckoldom was inseparable from Marriage... There is another accidental Advantage in Marriage... the having a Multitude of Children."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marriage is praised as conferring domestic authority (patriarchal sovereignty) and as an opportunity to impart virtuous education to many children; the writer argues that large, well-educated families offer increased chances for social advancement and civic/religious contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational fraternity and corrective custom among trades
rubrics_metrics.description: It was a Custom among them, whenever they saw a Brother tottering or unstable in his Post, to lend him a hand in order to settle him again therein:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trades and professions have informal corrective customs (mentorship, fraternité) to support inexperienced or failing members; though such practices may be a mix of helpfulness and the trade's own internal policing (the coachmen's 'endorsing' also contained rough treatment), they represent a communal standard for sustaining professional competence.
